title: Conscious sedation & general anaesthesia
blurb: IV midazolam and inhalation sedation, monitoring, escorts and aftercare, the sedation nurse's role and qualification, and how general anaesthesia differs.
question: A very anxious adult is booked for extractions under IV sedation. She arrives alone, saying a friend will collect her 'later', and plans to drive to work afterwards. During treatment her oxygen saturation reading starts to fall. What should happen at each point?

teach.body: Conscious sedation uses a drug, or drugs, to depress the central nervous system so treatment can be carried out, while verbal contact with the patient is kept throughout. The technique must have a wide enough margin of safety that loss of consciousness is unlikely. It helps anxious and phobic patients, people with a strong gag reflex, some patients with additional needs and those having longer or unpleasant procedures. It is not general anaesthesia, where the patient is unconscious.

teach.caption: Both are titrated: given in small steps until the patient is relaxed but responsive. Midazolam can also be given by other routes in specialist settings.

items.label: Blue: nitrous oxide
items.sub: Used with oxygen for inhalation sedation

teach.caption: Inhalation sedation machines won't deliver less than 30% oxygen, cut off nitrous oxide if the oxygen fails, and need active scavenging to protect staff from waste gas.

steps.label: Assessment visit
steps.sub: History, BP, suitability, written consent, written pre-op instructions

steps.label: On the day: checks
steps.sub: Escort present, history updated, baseline pulse, SpO₂, BP

steps.label: Treat & monitor
steps.sub: Clinical signs plus pulse oximeter throughout

steps.label: Discharge
steps.sub: To the escort, with written aftercare

teach.h: Monitoring: watch the patient and the machine
teach.body: The main danger of midazolam is respiratory depression: breathing slows and becomes shallow. Clinical monitoring means watching the level of consciousness, response to instructions, breathing rate and depth, and skin colour. A pulse oximeter measures oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and pulse throughout IV sedation, and blood pressure is taken before and after, and during if needed. Record readings on the sedation record. If SpO₂ falls, tell the sedationist at once: the patient is asked to breathe deeply, and oxygen and flumazenil are ready.

items.label: after IV sedation: no driving, alcohol, machinery or important decisions
trained people at least: the operator-sedationist and a trained sedation nurse
minimum oxygen an inhalation sedation machine delivers
oxygen saturation, monitored by pulse oximeter throughout

items: Hold an appropriate qualification, such as the NEBDN Certificate in Dental Sedation Nursing, or be training under supervision.
Check consent, escort, medical history and pre-op instructions before the patient is sedated.
Prepare cannulation equipment, the sedation drug, flumazenil, oxygen, suction and the emergency kit.
Monitor and record clinical signs and readings throughout, and reassure the patient.
Stay with the patient in recovery and tell the sedationist about any change.
Give verbal and written aftercare instructions to both the patient and the escort.

teach.body: After IV sedation the patient must leave with a responsible adult escort, who should stay with them, ideally travelling by car rather than public transport. For 24 hours they must not drive, cycle, operate machinery or cooking appliances, drink alcohol, sign legal documents or make important decisions, look after young children alone, or go back to work. Children having inhalation sedation also need a responsible adult with them. If there is no escort, IV sedation does not go ahead.

Under general anaesthesia (GA) the patient is unconscious, with no verbal contact and loss of protective reflexes, so the airway must be managed by an anaesthetist. In the UK, dental GA is only provided in a hospital setting with critical care facilities, never in a general dental practice. Patients follow strict fasting (nil by mouth) instructions and need an escort. GA is used, for example, for young children needing several extractions or patients who cannot cooperate with sedation.

teach.text: Flumazenil reverses midazolam, but it wears off sooner than midazolam does, so the patient can become sedated again. A patient given flumazenil must be kept and monitored for longer before discharge. Don't confuse it with naloxone, which reverses opioids.

items: Conscious sedation: verbal contact kept throughout; GA: unconscious, hospital only.
IV = midazolam, reversed by flumazenil. Inhalation = nitrous oxide and oxygen via nasal hood.
Monitor clinically plus pulse oximetry; BP before and after.
No escort, no IV sedation. 24 hours of restrictions afterwards.
Sedation nursing needs extra training and certification.

summary: You can now define conscious sedation, compare IV and inhalation techniques, describe the patient journey and the monitoring required, give correct escort and aftercare instructions, explain the sedation nurse's role and qualification, and say how general anaesthesia differs.

options: The airway is managed by a tube
A.why: In conscious sedation the patient stays able to respond to verbal commands throughout treatment.

whyNot.2: Sedation relaxes the patient but doesn't numb; local anaesthetic is still usually given.
whyNot.3: Airway tubes are used under general anaesthesia, not conscious sedation.

A.q: Which drug reverses the effects of IV midazolam?
A.why: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that reverses midazolam.

A.q: A patient booked for IV sedation arrives without an escort. What should happen?
options: Sedate her and keep her until she feels fine
Let her go home by taxi after treatment
Postpone the sedation until an escort is arranged
Use a smaller dose of midazolam instead
A.why: A responsible adult escort is essential after IV sedation, so treatment under sedation cannot go ahead without one.

whyNot.0: Feeling fine doesn't mean the drug has worn off; she still needs an escort.
whyNot.1: A taxi driver is not a responsible adult escort who will stay with her.
whyNot.3: Any IV sedation dose requires an escort; reducing it doesn't change that.

B.q: Which piece of equipment continuously measures oxygen saturation during IV sedation?
B.why: A pulse oximeter clipped to a finger shows oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and pulse rate continuously.

whyNot.2: A peak flow meter measures how fast someone can breathe out, used in asthma.

B.q: During inhalation sedation, which gases are delivered through the nasal hood?
B.why: Inhalation sedation uses a titrated mixture of nitrous oxide and oxygen.

whyNot.1: Carbon dioxide is not given for dental sedation.
whyNot.2: The machine mixes nitrous oxide with oxygen, not room air.
whyNot.3: Helium plays no part in dental sedation.

B.q: Which instruction should a patient be given for the 24 hours after IV sedation?
options: Return to work once you feel alert
Drive only if the journey is short
Do not sign any legal documents
A small glass of wine is fine
B.why: Midazolam affects judgement and memory, so patients must not make important decisions or sign legal documents for 24 hours.

whyNot.0: Patients should not return to work for the rest of the day, even if they feel alert.
whyNot.1: Patients must not drive at all for 24 hours.
whyNot.3: Alcohol must be avoided for 24 hours because it adds to the sedative effect.

C.q: What is the main risk of IV midazolam that the team monitors for?
C.why: Midazolam can slow and weaken breathing, which is why breathing and oxygen saturation are monitored closely.

whyNot.0: Midazolam doesn't typically raise blood sugar.
whyNot.2: Sedation tends to lower, not raise, blood pressure.
whyNot.3: Allergy is rare; respiratory depression is the key danger.

C.q: Where can dental treatment under general anaesthesia be provided in the UK?
options: Any practice with an oxygen supply
A practice with a sedation-trained nurse
A hospital with critical care facilities
A community clinic with a dentist present
C.why: Dental GA in the UK must take place in a hospital setting with critical care facilities.

whyNot.0: Oxygen alone doesn't make a practice suitable; GA isn't provided in practices.
whyNot.1: Sedation training doesn't permit GA in a practice.
whyNot.3: A dentist alone can't provide GA; an anaesthetist in a hospital setting is needed.

C.q: A patient was given flumazenil after becoming over-sedated. Why must they be monitored for longer before going home?
options: Flumazenil causes an allergic rash later
Flumazenil raises blood pressure for hours
Flumazenil makes the patient very hungry
Flumazenil can wear off before midazolam
C.why: Flumazenil acts for a shorter time than midazolam, so the patient can become re-sedated as it wears off.

whyNot.0: A delayed rash is not the reason for longer monitoring.
whyNot.1: Prolonged high blood pressure is not the concern; re-sedation is.
whyNot.2: Hunger is not a recognised reason to keep the patient.

reteach.title: Sedation is a dimmer switch, not an off switch
reteach.question: Think of a light on a dimmer. How does turning it down compare with switching it off, and what does that mean for sedation versus GA?

blocks.body: Conscious sedation is the dimmer turned down: the patient is relaxed and drowsy but still answers you. The sedationist turns the dial a little at a time (titration) and watches closely. If it goes too low, breathing slows, so you watch the patient and the pulse oximeter. Flumazenil turns the dimmer back up for midazolam; for gas, the nitrous oxide is turned off and oxygen given. GA is the switch off: unconscious, airway managed by an anaesthetist, and only in hospital.

bands.label: Too deep: slow breathing, falling SpO₂

blocks.text: If the patient stops responding to your voice, they are no longer consciously sedated. Tell the sedationist immediately.

explain.body: IV sedation uses midazolam through a cannula and is reversed by flumazenil. Inhalation sedation uses nitrous oxide and oxygen through a nasal hood, recovers quickly and is common for children.

test.q: Which sedation technique is most commonly used for anxious children in dental practice?
test.why: Inhalation sedation with nitrous oxide and oxygen is widely used for children because it is gentle and recovery is quick.

whyNot.0: IV sedation is mainly used for adults.
whyNot.2: GA is reserved for hospital and isn't a form of sedation.
whyNot.3: Oral diazepam is not the standard technique for children in practice.

explain.body: Watch consciousness, response, breathing and colour. Use a pulse oximeter throughout IV sedation for SpO₂ and pulse, and take blood pressure before and after. Record everything and report any fall in SpO₂ at once.

test.q: During IV sedation you notice the patient's breathing has become slow and shallow. What should you do first?
options: Write it down at the end of treatment
Turn the pulse oximeter off and on
Ask the escort to come in
test.why: Slow, shallow breathing is the main danger sign with midazolam and must be reported at once so it can be managed.

whyNot.1: Recording is important but the sedationist must be told straight away.
whyNot.2: The breathing problem is clinical; restarting the machine wastes time.
whyNot.3: The escort can't help manage the patient's breathing.

explain.body: No escort, no IV sedation. For 24 hours: no driving, alcohol, machinery, cooking, legal decisions, caring for children alone or work. Instructions are given verbally and in writing to patient and escort.

items.label: responsible adult escort who stays with the patient

test.q: Who should receive the written aftercare instructions after IV sedation?
options: Only the escort who collects them
test.why: The patient may not remember what was said because of midazolam's amnesic effect, so the escort is given the instructions too.

whyNot.0: The patient may not recall the advice, so the escort also needs it.
whyNot.1: The patient should still be given the instructions.
whyNot.3: The GP doesn't need routine aftercare instructions.

explain.body: Sedation nursing needs extra training and certification, such as the NEBDN Certificate in Dental Sedation Nursing. General anaesthesia means unconsciousness and is only given in hospital with critical care facilities.

test.q: Which qualification is designed for dental nurses who assist with conscious sedation?
options: NEBDN Certificate in Dental Sedation Nursing
NEBDN Certificate in Oral Health Education
NEBDN Certificate in Special Care Dental Nursing
test.why: The NEBDN Certificate in Dental Sedation Nursing is the post-registration qualification for sedation nursing.

whyNot.1: Oral Health Education covers prevention advice.
whyNot.3: Special Care Dental Nursing covers patients with additional needs.
